explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on “composite” name‐tokens that embed punctuation as separators—things like file‐ or module‐paths, import specifiers, locale tags, GUIDs/gene-IDs, hyphenated/underscored identifiers, etc. It flags any long alphanumeric token containing internal slashes, dots, hyphens or underscores that marks out a structured name or code.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature picks out tokens that are part of structured numeric metadata—street‐address numbers, timestamps (with colons), dates, phone numbers, etc. It fires on the digits and punctuation that form those formatted numeric entities.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on structured phone‐number–style digit sequences (groups of numbers in parentheses or separated by dots/hyphens), i.e. contact telephone numbers.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron marks out text that’s been put into bold‐face (i.e. surrounded by `**…**`) in markdown posts—it lights up on those emphasized words.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the “header” or top‐of‐file lines of code/config/snippet documents—things like import/package/using declarations, version or file‐format comments (e.g. charset, solution-file version, GLSL #version, pragma once), SQL/PL-pgSQL function headers, registry or batch script headers, XML prolog, Stack Overflow “Q:” lines, etc.—i.e. the metadata or directive lines that kick off a technical file or snippet.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects the “:” punctuation when it appears as the hour–minute delimiter in timestamps (e.g. “9:39 am,” “4:08 PM,” etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on non-restrictive relative-clause markers—particularly the pronoun “which” when it introduces an explanatory or parenthetical clause referring back to a preceding noun phrase or entire proposition. It flags the boundary where extra descriptive information (“which …”) is tacked on rather than essential to defining the head noun.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature is a detector for English negation in problem-reporting contexts—i.e. it fires strongly on “do/does/won’t … ’t” tokens (“don’t,” “doesn’t,” “won’t,” etc.), which typically signal failures, unmet conditions, or errors in troubleshooting text.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the boilerplate “preamble” lines of code and data files—things like file‐format/version/encoding declarations, import/define/pragma directives and other top-of-file metadata across languages.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature detects the “one-of-the…” superlative construction—phrases that mark an item as belonging to a highlighted subset (e.g. “one of the best/top/most…”).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on high‐level structural markers—things like section headings, horizontal rules or separators (===, ---), comment- or doc-metadata lines (#pragma, #…, /**…*/, “--- abstract:”), bold delimiters (**…**), etc.—i.e. the tokens that mark or emphasize the boundaries and titles of blocks in code or technical documents.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron detects document-level metadata and structural markers—things like titles/section headings, URLs and domain names, timestamps/dates, author or blog/forum headers—that typically appear in paper titles, blog posts or forum entries.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature is picking up the Markdown “answer” marker in Q&A posts—i.e. the bolded `A:` (double-asterisk) delimiter that signals the start of the answer section.
explanations.negative_explanation: The feature marks first-person self-reference—i.e. occurrences of “I” (and closely related personal voice) used by an author to introduce, narrate or frame personal statements in user-generated posts.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature flags English negation in the form of a contracted “n’t” (e.g. don’t, isn’t, weren’t) attached to auxiliaries or verbs.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on broad, abstract count‐nouns used to classify or quantify in formal/technical text—words like “types,” “kinds,” “number,” “variety,” “version,” “combination,” “use,” “amounts,” etc., that signal category or enumeration.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron seems to fire on the very tokens that close or terminate a logical unit—whether that’s the end of a code statement (e.g. “);” or “;”), the close of an XML/HTML tag (“>”), the colon after an email header (“Subject:”), or the last field in a data record.  In other words, it has learned a language-agnostic “end-of-unit” or “statement/record terminator” signal.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron lights up whenever the model is reading non-running-text “structural” chunks – things like titles/section headings, list or table rows (often ending in numbers or percent signs), image captions, code or template block delimiters, chapter markers, etc. In short, it flags formatted, metadata‐style lines rather than ordinary prose.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature is simply detecting the literal “**” token (two asterisks in a row), as used everywhere from Markdown/CSS comments to code-generated separators and legal-text page breaks.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron is a “structural‐marker” detector in factual or list­style prose.  It lights up on the tokens that frame out facts or enumerations—proper names and titles, dates or numerals (often in parentheses or with currency symbols), temporal/quantitative adverbs (over, past, nearly, last), connective words (and, not, a) and boundary punctuation (colons, dashes, periods).  In short, it flags the bits of text that set up or delimit chunks of concrete information.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on temporal anchors and sequence markers—timestamps, dates and their numeric components (e.g. “8:45 PM,” “18 67”), ordinals and position words (“first,” “last,” “former,” “past”), and similar tokens that locate or order events in time.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the little “directive” tokens that steer or structure code and markup—things like comment or emphasis delimiters (`**`, `!important`, `#…`), control-flow keywords (`break`, `for`, `catch`/`finally`), shell/Make commands (`MD`, `echo`, `Set`, `ok`), version or numeric flags in config files, etc. In other words, it spots the special punctuation and keywords that open, close or modify blocks, commands and formatting rather than ordinary identifiers.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron lights up on the “name” tokens in code and markup—i.e. the uppercase-led segments of identifiers, acronyms/initialisms or numeric IDs (PascalCase/CamelCase component and class names, XML tag names, acronyms like ACH/MPICC/SG, standalone digits in <id> etc.). It signals semantic boundaries in code-structured text.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the opening markers of top‐level code or documentation blocks—for example shebangs (`#!/…`), file‐header declarations (`<?php`, `"use strict"`), imports, function/class definitions, docstring or comment block starts, and StackOverflow “Q:” lines. It detects the boundary where a new high-level code unit or commentary section begins.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the discourse‐structuring “pivot” words—especially the main–clause verbs and linkers (e.g. saw, wanted, let, want, support, as, at, one) that introduce or frame the core action, intent or stance of a sentence. It thus marks the lexical cues authors use to launch a new point, report an event or state their purpose.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on “structural” or metadata-like tokens – things like version‐numbers (0, 1, 3, 11, 46.800, 07:55 GMT, etc.), record/ID numbers in XML or code, hostnames (e.g. imgur), timestamps, and other non-lexical identifiers (including the subword pieces of negation contractions like didn/aren/don/isn etc.). In short, it flags tokens that serve as external indexes or markers rather than carrying the sentence’s core propositional content.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron is a “directive‐or‐header” detector – it lights up on top‐level or block-level metadata/declaration lines (imports, includes, preprocessor/pragma directives, GFF “##” headers, email “Subject:”, JSON/CSS/SQL section headers, etc.) that introduce a file or configure a module. It abstracts the idea of “this line is declaring or configuring something for what follows.”
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on structured numeric tokens and temporal/metadata cues—things like clock times, dates, durations or version‐style codes (e.g. “06:06 a.m.,” “Sept. 14,” “3-hour,” “.mp4,” “2014 20:32 IST,” dollar amounts, percentages, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects top‐of‐file boilerplate or “header” declarations—things like encoding/charset directives, import/using/namespace/package/version/pragma statements, macro or registry key definitions, file‐metadata comments, etc.—across many languages.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron flags words that occur in high‐level document headings or titles—i.e. tokens in section headers, article/paper titles, menus or other structural labels.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the standard legal‐boilerplate you find at the top of source files—e.g. commented “Copyright (c) YEAR … All rights reserved” lines and the accompanying redistribution‐and‐license terms.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron flags discourse‐structuring tokens—common function words, connective particles, punctuation and adverbs (e.g. “It,” “and,” “in,” “which,” “very,” commas, etc.) that introduce or link clauses and mark sentence boundaries.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on bits of “chrome” or metadata in a page—section‐labels, captions and other non-prose headers (e.g. “Contact Information,” “Photo:,” “Poll Question,” “Description,” “CALL:,” “Menu,” etc.) rather than the running body text.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron seems to fire on the “main entity” of a sentence in formal, scientific prose—i.e. the head noun (or occasional relative pronoun) that names the thing under study or being described (populations, structures, chips, receptors, patients, pathogens, “which/that/who” introducing their modifiers, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects the final subword of a multi‐part identifier—e.g. the trailing segment of a domain name, XML/HTML tag, version string or other slash‐/dot‐delimited token—i.e. it marks the suffix at the end of a structured token.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on “top‐of‐file” or “section‐prologue” markers across languages: import/using/namespace declarations, XML/HTML prologues and tags (<?php>, <?xml>, <…>), question headers (Q:), etc.—i.e. tokens that open a new file or major block.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on “field” or “delimiter” tokens that mark out structured data in text—e.g. XML/HTML tag names, URL/domain or path segments, package==version entries, list-item labels or citation keys—essentially signaling the boundaries and labels of templated, semi-structured content.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on mentions of the monocyte–macrophage lineage—that is, tokens and stems like “macrophage(s)” referring to macrophage immune cells.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron detects “top-of-file” boilerplate or preamble constructs across many languages—things like version/package directives, import/include statements, license/author tags, shebangs, XML prologues, namespace or module headers, and similar metadata-setting lines.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron detects the boundaries (and content) of high-level titles or section headings—i.e. the marked‐up, often bolded or specially delimited, line that names a document, page, product, question, video, code interface, etc.
